A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TRACE research. The main text and appendices are readable, and retained methods, experiments, equations and figures can be matched despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

before.justification: V1 reports original human-preference evaluations, capability benchmarks, adversarial tests and synthetic policy-agreement results in Tables 1–4.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds component ablations, comparator experiments, oracle-sensitivity tests, sequential updates and model-level results.

M1.justification: The three-stage framework, hybrid losses and optional corrective oracle remain. However, v2's Eq. 9 and Algorithm 1 revise the specified procedure to weight both conflict classes, clip negative weights, correct retain-set membership and suppress both responses in the non-oracle branch. These are procedural corrections and refinements within the existing method.

E1.justification: Within the retained datasets and capability benchmarks, v2 substantially broadens policy-update scenarios. Appendix A.5 evaluates an alternative Red-Team Analyst policy and a Base–Strict–Revert lifecycle; A.12 adds an IP-only policy shift. These introduce different policy requirements and sequential adaptation beyond v1's original evaluations.

E2.justification: V2 adds Naive Oracle DPO as a matched-oracle comparator in the data-scale and weak-oracle experiments (Tables 5 and 18), and robust DPO, rDPO, in the noisy-oracle comparison (Table 16). These substantially expand comparison beyond the retained U2A and DPO-Gold baselines, testing whether ordinary oracle relabeling or robust preference optimization explains TRACE's benefits.

E3.justification: V1 Section 5.2 describes transforming a new-policy model back toward the old policy; v2 Section 6.2 instead starts from the old-policy model and targets the new policy. This is a substantive reported protocol revision, without establishing that retained results were rerun. New experiments also introduce 5k/10k/20k data budgets, 10%/20% label corruption, weaker-oracle controls and sparse-conflict testing.

E4.justification: V1 contains adversarial tests and qualitative examples but no component ablations. V2 adds uniform-weighting and triage/KL-removal ablations, sample-efficiency comparisons, alternative and sequential policy tests, oracle-noise and weak-oracle sensitivity, and sparse-conflict analysis (Sections 5.5, 7.3 and A.4–A.12). It also reports quantitative oracle-audit findings.

E5.justification: V2 Table 10 adds uncertainty values to model-level human-preference win rates, whereas v1 reports those evaluations as point estimates. The existing 95% confidence-interval practice is retained, but v1 Table 2's explicit statement that results average three runs disappears. The PDFs do not establish a change in the actual number of runs.

E6.justification: U2A's PKU-SafeRLHF win rate against TRACE changes from 12.9% to 18.2% (v1 Table 1; v2 Table 2), while the original aggregate capability and attack scores remain unchanged. V2 adds extensive ablation, model-level, noise, lifecycle and comparator results; Table 5, for example, reports 70.7% versus 52.2% agreement for TRACE versus Naive DPO on Llama-3.1-8B at 20k samples. Some added breakdowns conflict with retained aggregates, notably Tables 11 and 3.

T1.justification: The influence-function argument and Hessian approximation are retained. V2 corrects the formal aggregate objective, adds a conflict-ratio definition in Eq. 10 and supplies a computational-cost analysis in A.9. There is no new theorem or proof establishing the newly asserted information-theoretic robustness limit.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains policy-driven re-alignment using existing preference data. V2's conclusion qualifies v1's near-gold-standard quality and negligible-utility-loss claims by acknowledging a HellaSwag trade-off and residual adversarial gap, while newly attributing that gap to an information-theoretic limit. These refine the retained claims, although the abstract still claims no general-utility degradation.

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands interpretation and applicability boundaries: weighting is described as a gradient filter, KL as a utility anchor, and U2A's lower fictional-scenario ASR as an over-refusal effect. Sections 7.2–7.4 and A.1 discuss utility trade-offs, deployment priorities and the untested fully blind setting; A.10–A.12 interpret oracle and conflict sensitivity. The claimed unavoidable information-theoretic limit exceeds what the supplied analysis establishes.

D1.justification: V2 newly discloses oracle implementation details, three annotators per response triplet, attack templates and a 400-prompt adversarial evaluation protocol. Appendix A.9 adds three RTX A6000 GPUs, training-time and memory figures, and computational overhead; the abstract adds a code-release link. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation without establishing changes to previously used settings.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands positioning around industrial annotation guidelines, regulatory governance and policy-aware correction versus influence-based data retrieval. It adds discussion and citations concerning TRAK, influence-function fragility, robust DPO and non-binary preferences, alongside additional RLHF and governance literature. The earlier benchmark and alignment-method discussion largely remains.

P1.justification: V2 substantially rewrites the abstract, introduction and method exposition, introduces a standalone realignment-problem section, and separates experimental setup from results. The appendix gains organized mechanism, robustness, oracle and computational sections. This is extensive narrative restructuring beyond the addition of experiments.

P2.justification: V2 changes the document from single-column to two-column presentation, redistributes the original result tables and splits Algorithm 1 across pages. The original SynthValueBench policy figures move to the appendix as Figures 11–12; new policy figures and numerous ablation and model-level tables are added. Existing qualitative examples remain but are reformatted.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important gaps in v1 through algorithm corrections, matched-oracle controls, ablations and reproducibility details. However, its added evidence introduces unresolved contradictions: Table 11 gives TRACE a SynthValueBench GSM8K average of 70.4 versus Table 3's 69.5, and Table 13 claims superiority to full retraining despite reporting 76.7% for TRACE versus 79.8% for DPO-Gold. Section 4.1 and A.1 also disagree about requiring the old policy specification. These affect central results and applicability, preventing a reliable net-quality judgment.
